# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
# Review of "Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations"

This is a strong follow-up. It does most of what the earlier reviews asked for:
- **Hours:** it checks timesheets against system logs.
- **Mediation:** it registers the mediation test before the 24-month outcomes were available.
- **Counter offices:** it reports the end of the counter arm with control-group waits and a cost estimate.
- **Halden subset:** it calls the Halden survivors "survivors twice over."
- **Earlier claims:** it answers both the re-analysis and the meta-analysis with evidence.

Section 5's point about the meta-analysis is decisive. The four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, which confirms that the "no decay" claim could not be supported.

The main problems are:
- **Mediation:** "confirms" is too strong.
- **Log-hours measure:** what it actually records is unclear.
- **Control contamination:** the meeting audit in two control offices may explain part of the decline but isn't analysed.
- **Summary:** it compares two different hours measures.

## Arithmetic

The figures are internally consistent:
- **Varden per-hour gains:** 0.966/0.88 = 1.098, i.e. +9.8% on timesheets; 0.966/0.89 = 1.085, i.e. +8.5% on logs. The confidence intervals are symmetric on the log scale.
- **Mediation shares:** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.
- **Halden continuers:** 34.9/40.3 = 0.866, i.e. −13.4% hours; 96.8/86.6 = 1.118, i.e. +11.8% per hour.
- **"Declined by about a quarter":** 12.5% → 9.8% is a 22% decline.
- **Counter staffing:** restoring capacity after −17% hours and +6.7% per hour needs about 1/(0.83 × 1.067) ≈ 1.13, roughly 13% more staff. That matches the county's 12%.

## Main issues

**1. The Summary compares two different hours measures.**
- It reports a fall "from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." The 12.5% uses timesheets; the 8.5% uses logs.
- The like-for-like comparison, given in the body, is **12.5% → 9.8%**. The Summary overstates the decline, which is unusual given that the error runs against the authors' own result.
- The Summary should report the timesheet comparison, with 8.5% as the log-based figure at 24 months.
- No test of the change itself is reported. The intervals overlap heavily (+6.9 to +18.4 versus +4.6 to +15.2), and the estimates come from the same offices, so their errors are correlated. "Consistent with some fading" is the right phrasing; a formal test would show how firm it is.

**2. It is unclear what the log-hours measure records, and this affects the mediation result.**
- The logs are described as recording "time staff are working on cases."
- If that is literally true, log-measured hours should exclude meetings. Treated offices cut about 3.5 hours of meetings per week, so case time should have fallen much less than total hours:
  - Roughly: total hours went from 37.9 to about 33.4, and meetings from 7.4 to 3.9.
  - Non-meeting time therefore fell only about 3%, from 30.5 to 29.5 hours.
  - Yet log hours fell 11%.
- So either the logs capture something closer to total logged-in time (including meetings), or the figures don't match the description.
- This matters for interpreting the mediation result:
  - If the denominator is *time spent on cases*, cutting meetings cannot raise output per log-hour simply by freeing time. It would have to work through fewer interruptions or better focus.
  - If the denominator is total time, the "freed time" explanation applies.
- The paper should define the measure precisely. It should also confirm that pre-trial log data exist, because a difference-in-differences on log hours needs a baseline. The log measure was "added" at follow-up.

**3. "Confirms" is too strong for the mediation result.**
- **Not an independent test.** The meetings hypothesis came from the seven treated offices, and the "confirmatory" test uses the same seven offices over a longer window. Pre-registration reduces analytic flexibility, but it does not make this an independent replication.
- **Registration timing.** The test was registered at month 11, after the nine-month results were known. The paper should state which months the 24-month outcome covers. If it includes months 1–11, part of the outcome had already been observed when the test was registered.
- **Effective sample size.** "A larger sample of office-months" does not increase it. The units are 14 offices, and the confidence intervals (28–66%, 2–34%) should be checked for this. A wild-cluster bootstrap or randomisation-based inference would be appropriate.
- **Model assumptions.** The paper names the main assumption: no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome. It does not address two others:
  - **Mediator ordering:** meeting cuts plausibly reduce fatigue, so the 47%/18% split depends on whether the two mediators were modelled jointly or in sequence.
  - **Temporal order:** mediators and outcome were measured over the same period.
- The body's word, "survives," is accurate. The Summary's "confirms" should be changed to match it.

**4. Two control offices cut their own meetings, and the trial estimates don't account for this.**
- At month 15, two control offices cut meeting time from 7.1 to 5.0 hours and gained 4.1% in output per hour. This narrows the treated–control gap after month 15.
- Rough size: 4.1% × 2/7 ≈ **1.2 points** on the control mean in those months. That could explain a meaningful share of the 2.7-point decline from 12.5% to 9.8%.
- Part of the apparent "fading" may therefore be control offices improving, not treated offices fading.
- **Needed:** a sensitivity analysis excluding those two offices, or splitting the period at month 15.
- The arithmetic also implies something unexplained. The control mean moved only from 7.2 to 7.0. If two offices fell by 2.1 hours each, the other five must have *risen* by about 0.56 hours each. That should be confirmed and explained.
- The audit itself may have been prompted by the trial. Control offices knew about it, and the nine-month report flagged that awareness as a risk.

**5. Backlog and time-to-decision are still not reported.**
- Output per FTE is −3.4% (CI −8.0 to +1.2) and has edged down since nine months.
- In queue-based work, a small persistent shortfall can show up as growing backlogs or longer processing times rather than lower case closures. The nine-month report named this as a risk.
- The case-management system holds the data, and two years is long enough for any build-up to be visible.

## Halden section

- **The reverters are not all coverage-bound.** The Summary says the three reverters all had "client-facing or coverage obligations." But the marketing agency cited **client deadlines**, which is discretionary work in the meta-analysis's coding. Grouping it with coverage cases hides the finding that discretionary settings can also fail.
- **"Upper bound" is too strong.** The continuers are probably an overestimate because they are double survivors, and response to the follow-up request (14 of 23) adds a third layer of selection. But with no comparison group, two years of background change are also in the figures, including wider changes in workplace tools over 2023–25, and those could push the estimate either way. "Likely an overestimate" is defensible; a strict upper bound is not.
- **Halden's attrition is left unaddressed.** A Halden author co-signs this report, but it does not respond to the re-analysis's finding that seven of the nine withdrawals happened after the schedule began, mostly citing workload. Section 5 answers the "entirely artifact" claim but not this documented misdescription.

## Smaller points

- **No confidence intervals** are given for sick days (−27%), resignations or the appeal rate. The earlier caution about imprecision with few offices still applies.
- **Appeal-overturn rates** at 24 months now cover decisions old enough to have been appealed, which addresses the earlier lag concern. The 0.2-point gap (3.2% v 3.0%) still needs an interval.
- **The meeting-audit observation** is appropriately hedged. The trial cannot tell whether reorganising alone would capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes reorganisation happen and stick. That is the most useful open question here. A future trial with a "reorganise only" arm would answer it.

## How the five documents fit together

| Source | Per-hour gain, discretionary work | Coverage-bound work | Durability | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Halden (pilot) | +23.4% (scheduled hours, manager-reported) | Claimed sector-general | 6 months | Fatigue (asserted) |
| Varden (9 months) | +12.5% | Per worker −11.4% | 9 months | Meetings (exploratory) |
| Varga & Holm | +10.8%, then "entirely artifact" | Retail −11.2% | Argues novelty | Dismisses meetings |
| Meta-analysis | About 8–10% (controlled / bias-adjusted) | Per worker −8.9% | "No decay" (unsupported) | Fatigue correlation weak; meetings untested |
| **Varden (24 months)** | **+9.8% (timesheets), +8.5% (logs)** | **Arm ended; +12% staff needed** | **About 22% decline, not to zero** | **Meetings about half, fatigue about a fifth (same offices)** |

The evidence is now fairly coherent:
- **Discretionary work:** a gain of roughly 8–10% per actual hour persists to two years, with some fading. Output per worker stays slightly below control.
- **Coverage-bound work:** with fixed staffing, the scheme doesn't hold. Keeping service levels costs about 9% more per contact.
- **Mechanism:** most of the explained gain looks organisational (fewer meetings) rather than rest. That rests on one employer's seven offices and depends on mediation assumptions.
- **Main open question:** whether the gain needs the hours cut at all, or only the reorganisation it prompts.

I can turn this into a consolidated evidence summary across all five documents, or draft referee comments for this report.
